executive_assessment.text: Named 2023/24 drought and flood examples distinguish meteorological conditions from household losses and later recovery constraints.
Economic stress, unequal control over resources and weak protection services form a plausible protection-risk mechanism, but reported cases and forecasts are not causal estimates.
Dzaleka/host payouts and district preparedness outputs are documented without assuming sustained resilience gains.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2025-04-01 reports: In the 2023/24 season, meteorological drought lasted five months in Machinga, Mangochi, Zomba and Chikwawa, and four months in Chitipa, Nsanje, Dedza, Phalombe, Chiradzulu and Thyolo; additional southern and central districts had dry spells through much of the season.

Source dated 2025-04-01 reports: For the 2023/24 season, DoDMA data in the report count 17,033 households affected by floods in Karonga and Nkhotakota; all recorded hazards affected 21,333 households.

The July 2024 UN assessment cites a rapid gender analysis linking deprivation to exploitation risk and weak local protection services; Machinga recorded 286 child marriages in January–May 2024 versus 162 a year earlier.

Source dated 2025-04-07 reports: The CCA reports 20,000+ people displaced by March 2024 floods in Karonga and Nkhotakota; about 400 households remained displaced in Nsanje, Chikwawa, Zomba and Nkhotakota; early camp closures prompted returns to unrepaired, flood-exposed homes.

Source dated 2025-04-07 reports: After dry spells and food insecurity, mostly male members of drought-affected Southern Region households moved semi-voluntarily for casual work in Blantyre, Mzuzu, Lilongwe, Rumphi or Mzimba.

Source dated not stated reports: WFP and UNHCR reported that about 4,000 households affected by El Niño in Dzaleka refugee camp and its host community received a US$400,000 parametric-insurance payout in 2024.
UNICEF's January 2026 report says 11 districts exceeded 2025 severe-wasting projections, naming Neno, Nsanje and Chikwawa; these are service/planning indicators, not district prevalence estimates.

Source dated 2026-01-26 reports: UNICEF reported deep-water systems in drought-affected schools and communities in Nsanje and Neno reaching over 12,000 people, more than half women and girls; improved sanitation reached 36,569 people in Chikwawa and Nsanje.

known_gaps.text: Automated machine-screening is not independent source verification or human approval. 19 of 19 evidence records and 1 of 1 pathways lack claim-level verification in this remediation; review the linked records before relying on them.
Malawi's 2025 BTR/Fourth National Communication could not be opened because of its file size; claims from it are not used.
Draft collection pending human source review and approval. IDA eligibility is not an FCV classification.
National and selected local examples do not establish district-level coverage or causal attribution.
No inspected source establishes climate as a cause of armed violence in Malawi; the CCA's future host–migrant tension pathway is conditional, not an incident-level finding.
Protection and GBV findings in the 2024 El Niño assessment are secondary synthesis and may be underreported; named-district detail is limited.
The 2024 UN Country Results Report and 2025 UNICEF report describe outputs and historical conditions, not evaluated effects or current 2026 coverage.
The CCA identifies climate-related mobility and land competition but does not quantify future conflict risk by district or provide a climate scenario.
The Machinga marriage counts are reported cases from secondary rapid-analysis evidence, not prevalence, and cannot identify an El Niño causal effect.
No inspected source establishes current host–migrant violence or evaluates whether training, plans or parametric payouts reduced long-term vulnerability.
Draft extension: human source review and approval remain pending. Lending eligibility is not an FCV classification.
